questions.question: What are blocks and yield in Ruby?
questions.title: Blocks and Yield in Ruby
questions.direct_answer: A block is a chunk of code you pass to a method: [1,2,3].each { |x| puts x } (do...end for multi-line). The method runs the block with `yield`: def twice; yield; yield; end; twice { puts 'hi' } prints hi twice. yield can pass arguments: def map_to; yield 10; end; map_to { |n| n * 2 } returns 20 (yield's value becomes the block's return). A method checks for a block with block_given?. Use { } for single-line, do/end for multi-line (precedence: {} binds tighter to the left). Blocks are closures — they capture surrounding variables. They're how Ruby does iteration (each/map), callbacks, and DSLs. yield is the call; the block is the code you pass; &block captures the block as a Proc.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know a block is a chunk of code passed to a method, yield runs it, and yield can pass arguments.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using do/end where {} is needed (precedence) — or forgetting block_given? before yielding.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Blocks = chunks of code passed to methods ({} or do/end). yield runs the block; yield can pass args. block_given? checks. Blocks are closures.

sections.title: Blocks + yield
sections.content:
block = chunk of code; yield runs it; yield can pass args. block_given? checks. Closures.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M[method] --> Y[yield: run the block]
  Y --> A[pass args: yield 10]
  B[block {|n| n*2}] --> R[returns to yield]
  C[block_given?] --> G[yield only if block given]
```

sections.title: Blocks and yield
sections.content:
```ruby
# A block: a chunk of code passed to a method
[1, 2, 3].each { |x| puts x }      # single-line: { ... }
[1, 2, 3].each do |x|               # multi-line: do ... end
  puts x
end

# `yield` runs the block (possibly multiple times):
def twice
  yield
  yield
end
twice { puts 'hi' }                  # hi hi

# yield can PASS arguments (the block returns a value to yield):
def map_to
  result = yield 10                 # passes 10 to the block
  puts result                       # the block's return
end
map_to { |n| n * 2 }                 # 20

# block_given? checks if a block was passed:
def maybe
  return 'no block' unless block_given?
  yield
end
maybe { 'ran' }                     # 'ran'
maybe                               # 'no block'

# Blocks are CLOSURES (capture surrounding variables):
n = 10
[1, 2].each { |x| puts x + n }      # n captured from outside

# {} binds tighter to the left than do/end (precedence):
#   puts [1,2].map { |x| x }  vs  puts [1,2].map do |x| x end
# &block captures the block as a Proc:
def capture(&block); block.call; end
capture { 'hi' }                    # 'hi'
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using do/end where {} is needed (precedence differs).
Forgetting block_given? before yielding (yield without a block raises).
Confusing yield (runs the block) with return (exits the method).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A block is a chunk of code passed to a method ({} or do...end).
yield runs the block; yield can pass arguments to it.
block_given? checks if a block was passed (yield without a block raises).
Use { } for single-line, do/end for multi-line; {} binds tighter to the left.
Blocks are closures (capture surrounding variables); &block captures as a Proc.

sections.content: A block is a chunk of code you pass to a method: 1 2 3 dot each block x puts x (do end for multi-line). The method runs the block with yield: def twice; yield; yield; end; twice block puts hi prints hi twice. yield can pass arguments: def map_to; yield 10; end; map_to block n n times 2 returns 20 (yield's value becomes the block's return). A method checks for a block with block_given question. Use braces for single-line, do end for multi-line (precedence: braces bind tighter to the left). Blocks are closures — they capture surrounding variables. They're how Ruby does iteration (each/map), callbacks, and DSLs. yield is the call; the block is the code you pass; ampersand block captures the block as a Proc. A common mistake is using do end where braces are needed for precedence, and forgetting block_given before yielding, since yield without a block raises.
